units.title: OP Stack chains with ETH gas
angles: Exits. Can an ordinary account make another user's swap or liquidity removal impossible to include or always revert on this network (gas caps, storage pricing, per-transaction limits, tick crossing cost, special recipients)?

Known weaknesses. Collect security advisories, audit reports, bug bounty write-ups, incident post-mortems and open issues for this network's execution client, precompiles and system contracts from the last two years, including behaviour the network calls by design. For each, decide whether an ordinary account could use it against funds in the PoolManager.

units.title: Stablecoin-native L1s
angles: Faces. Find every way one balance at the PoolManager can be reached under two currency ids or in two units on this network (native asset with an ERC-20 face, wrapped native predeploys, bridged and canonical versions sharing storage, tokens with more than one entry point), and walk sync, settle, take, mint and burn across the two faces in every order.

Pooled assets. Read the PoolManager's largest token balances on this network from chain. For each token, check transfer and balanceOf for behaviour any holder can trigger: rebasing, fees, callbacks, share accounting, special recipients, special amounts.

units.title: HyperEVM
angles: Upcoming forks. Assume every network upgrade scheduled or proposed for the next six months ships. What changes for the PoolManager and for funds already inside it, and what could an ordinary account do the day after?

Opcode differential. For each opcode and call pattern the PoolManager relies on (TSTORE and TLOAD including rollback on revert and clearing at transaction end, CALL with value, CALLVALUE, SELFBALANCE, STATICCALL, RETURNDATASIZE and RETURNDATACOPY, MCOPY, PUSH0, gas forwarding, calls to addresses without code, precompile dispatch), read this network's execution client source and find where it departs from Ethereum's behaviour.

Inherited caller. The PoolManager calls code that an ordinary account controls in three places: the unlock callback, a hook, and the recipient of a native take. In each of them msg.sender is the PoolManager. From such a frame, test every precompile, system contract and token that the node implements in native code on this network with DELEGATECALL, CALLCODE and STATICCALL as well as CALL, by eth_call with a forwarding stub placed at the PoolManager address by state override and a second stub as the callee. Does any of them act on the account of the inherited caller, or accept a stated value that no balance backs? Read the dispatch code of the client for each one that does not revert.

units.title: High-throughput chains with modified gas models
angles: Sweep. List every precompile, predeploy, system contract, face of the native asset, wrapped native token, bridge, staking and fee contract on this network. For each one, run eth_call with "from" set to the PoolManager address for the call shapes P1, P2, P3 and P5 in ASSUMPTIONS.md (empty calldata with zero value, transfer(address,uint256) with zero and nonzero amount, balanceOf(PoolManager), and each IHooks selector), and record what comes back. Follow up on every target that does not revert.

Transaction types. For every transaction type and execution context this network adds (batches, sponsored or fee-token transactions, deposits, retryables, system calls, account abstraction, delegated accounts), work out what msg.sender, msg.value and transient storage look like inside the PoolManager and walk unlock, sync, settle and take through each.

code.task: The five audit reports in docs/security/audits are documents of this repository and a permitted reference for what the source is meant to do. Read them with the Read tool (it opens PDF files; pass a page range of at most 20 pages per call). Never fetch or compare against any other copy of the code. For every finding of the reports assigned to you, including informational ones, write one result: the hazard in one sentence; the statement in src/ that closes it today with file and line, read by you, or the fact that nothing in src/ closes it; the properties of the chain or of a token that the closing statement relies on (ASSUMPTIONS.md A1 to A14); and whether that reliance holds on each of the 21 networks, using state/networks.json, state/cleared.json and your own read-only queries where the ledger has no answer. Where a report describes a fix, a recommendation that the team accepted, or the text of the code at the time, check that the present text of src/ has the property the fix was meant to give, by reading src/ only. A finding whose fix is absent, weaker than described, or dependent on a network property that fails on one of the 21 networks is the most valuable thing you can report. Put closed findings in "cleared" (one entry per audit finding, with the audit name and finding number in "check"), anything open in "findings" or "leads". Start with the findings that name a property of a chain or of a token. Your reports: OpenZeppelin_audit_core.pdf and TrailOfBits_audit_core.pdf, and after them docs/security/Known_Effects_of_Hook_Permissions.pdf, where each listed effect takes the place of a finding. This answers lead L-482 for these two reports.

Leads L-463 and L-458, with L-464 as a method rule. Part one (L-463): find pooled tokens whose transfer lowers the sender's balance by more than the amount, for some recipient. WHITE on Ethereum (F-092) charges the sender 10 percent on top when the recipient is its listed v2 style pair, and it was found only through its transaction history. Take every priced currency of every network from the price lists and currency lists in cycles/005 and cycles/006 work directories (theme-assigned-balance.work, theme-currency-lists.work, theme-token-triggers.work), find its v2 style pairs, v3 pools and any address its code names as pair, market, exchange or taxed recipient, and simulate transfer from the PoolManager address to each of them with a measuring stub placed by state override, as theme-currency-lists did. Report every token where the PoolManager balance falls by more than the amount, the size of the surcharge, whether the full amount can be brought back to the PoolManager at no cost (skim on a v2 pair, or a transfer from the pair that arrives in full), the pooled balance and its value. Part two (L-458): list every pooled vault, receipt, staking or migration token on all 21 networks that has a function taking the holder as an argument (claimFor, migrateFor, redeemFor, exitFor, convertFor, withdrawTo with an owner argument, upgradeFor, wrapFor, depositFor that burns the old token, and names like them), call each with the PoolManager as the holder from an unrelated address by eth_call, and report every call that changes balanceOf(PoolManager) of a pooled token. ibBUSD on BNB Smart Chain (F-090) is the known case. Start with currencies worth more than 1,000 USD at a PoolManager and go down from there. Method rule (L-464): a verifier found that bsc.api.pocket.network silently dropped 132 of 323 logs in a whole history scan. Do not rely on one log endpoint for a count on BNB Smart Chain; check each count against a second source or against a value that does not depend on logs. For each token found, say whether an ordinary account gains, or whether the effect is a loss or a freeze for the liquidity providers of that token's pools, and whether the cause is the token or a property of the network.
